details:
**Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar**
Job's three friends, often called his "comforters," who sit silently with him in mourning for seven days and nights. After Job curses the day he was born, they argue in long speeches that he must have sinned to deserve his suffering; Eliphaz the Temanite speaks first, and Bildad the Shuhite insists that "God will not cast away a perfect man."

**Elihu**
A young man who appears unannounced after Job and his three friends have finished arguing. He says he held back out of respect for his elders but declares that "great men are not always wise," rebukes both Job and the friends, and defends God's justice; the voice from the whirlwind follows his speech.

**Behemoth and Leviathan**
Two mighty creatures that God describes to Job to show the limits of human power. Behemoth, called "the chief of the ways of God," has bones like "tubes of bronze" and can draw the Jordan into his mouth (Thomas Aquinas thought it was an elephant), and God asks, "Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?" Jewish legend pairs them with a third monster, the bird Ziz, which the book does not mention.

**Voice from the whirlwind**
God's reply to Job, spoken out of a whirlwind (storm) in two speeches, beginning with the command "Gird up now thy loins like a man." God asks, "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" and overwhelms Job with questions about creation, after which Job repents.

**"Naked came I out of my mother's womb"**
Job's response to losing his children and possessions: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord."

**Wager between God and Satan**
The book's opening frame, in which God praises Job as "perfect and upright" and Satan ("the adversary") argues that Job is pious only because he is prosperous. God allows Satan to take away Job's wealth, children, and health to test whether he will curse God.

**"Curse God, and die"**
The only words spoken by Job's wife, who asks, "Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die." Job rebukes her as speaking like a foolish woman and refuses to sin with his lips.

**Boils**
Satan's second affliction, in which Job is struck with sore boils from head to foot. Job sits among the ashes and scrapes himself with a shard of pottery (a potsherd).

**"I know that my redeemer liveth"**
Job's declaration of faith in Job 19: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." It is famously set as a soprano aria in Handel's Messiah and inspired a well-known hymn.

**"I only am escaped alone to tell thee"**
The refrain of the four messengers who arrive one after another in Job 1 to report disasters: raiders stealing his oxen and camels, fire from heaven burning his sheep, and a great wind collapsing a house on his seven sons and three daughters. The line is also the epigraph of the epilogue of Moby-Dick.

**Land of Uz**
The place where Job lived, described as "the greatest of all the men of the east." Before his trials he owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred donkeys.

**"Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward"**
A line from Eliphaz's first speech, arguing that suffering is a natural part of human life and that Job should seek God.

**Pharaoh's three advisers**
A rabbinic tradition in the Talmud holds that Job, Balaam, and Jethro were advisers to Pharaoh when he decreed the killing of newborn Hebrew boys. Balaam supported the plan, Jethro fled, and Job remained silent, so he was later punished with suffering.

**"By the skin of my teeth"**
A phrase that originates in Job 19:20, where Job says, "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth," describing how close he has come to destruction.

**Job's restoration**
At the end of the book, God rebukes the three friends, and Job prays for them. God restores Job's fortune twofold and gives him seven new sons and three daughters, Jemima, Keziah, and Keren-happuch, the most beautiful women in the land.
